newsitem.title: DENMARK: FEATURE - Danish royal house sees red over nude pictures.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Danish royal house sees red over nude pictures.

text.p: Nude holiday pictures of Denmark's Crown Prince Frederik in a Stockholm tabloid have enraged the royal court and revived Danish press attacks against neighbouring Sweden.

Stockholm's Aftonbladet on Thursday showed photographs of Queen Margrethe's eldest son diving naked into a pool from a window of a family castle in southern France with the caption "what would mummy say Crown Prince Frederik ?"

More pictures inside the paper are accompanied by text saying that waiting in the pool below, also naked, is Danish pop singer Maria Montell, 28, whom the media have been romantically linking with the 29-year-old prince throughout the summer.

"I have not seen the pictures...but it is offensive to do such a thing," Frederik's court chief Per Thornit told Reuters, adding that clothed pictures of the couple which appeared at home were no less an invasion of privacy.

Danish newspapers published more sedate pictures of the couple in swimwear, shot by the same paparazzi photographer from outside the grounds of the Chateau de Caix, owned by Frederik's French-born father, Prince Henrik.
Even those caused something of a stir at home, where publication of such shots is rare.

Although taking photographs of subjects on private property is an offence under Danish law, the court would take no action, Thornit said. Tradition against taking the royal family to court meant also that it could not sue others.
But there was nothing to prevent Montell, or friends of the couple included in some of the pictures, from issuing writs, he added. "Its up to them, if they feel offended they can do what they like."

The pictures are much milder than many which have appeared of the scandal-ridden British royals and arguably less offensive than local media jokes, many of them aimed at the foreign-born spouses of the royal family.

Henrik was fiercely lampooned during his early years as consort and when Frederik's brother Joachim announced his engagement to Hong-Kong born Alexandra Manley a weekly tv show referred to her as "the spring roll."
The satirical magazine Svikmoellen tells how Joachim was accused of a bomb plot:
"Security men found a Chinese cracker in his bed," it wrote. "Fortunately the plot failed as the cracker was found to be wet."
The daily broadsheet Politiken's jokey back page recently had fun with the Crown Prince and Maria, saying that while he had been reported on a recent trip to be in a motel, he was in fact on Montell.
SCORN FOR SWEDISH DISRESPECT
But while Danish papers are free to take such liberties, woe betide a disrespectful foreigner, especially a Swede.
"Those bloody Swedes are attacking our royal family again," grumbled Ekstra Bladet.

"The mighty Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet has made a declaration of war against Denmark. The paper showed several pictures of our Crown Prince Frederik in the bare buff with his crown jewels on display," it added.

Denmark has a national chip on its shoulder toward Sweden, bigger geographically and with more than 50 percent more citizens than its neighbour now, but once the smaller brother when Denmark ruled large tracts of Sweden, Germany and Norway.
Save for a few islands, Denmark lost its Swedish possessions in the 17th century after a series of wars.
There is also lingering resentment at neutral Sweden's co-operation with Germany during World War Two, when Denmark was under Nazi occupation.
Feelings were last bruised in January, when Sweden's Gothenburg Post criticised Queen Margrethe's public smoking.
Ekstra Bladet declared a "smoke war against the Swedes" and other newspapers told Sweden to mind its own business.
